Taste of NC celebrates Tryon’s wine heritage 

Published 2:00 pm Tuesday, November 10, 2026

By Steven W. Siler

More than 200 guests attended Taste of NC, an evening devoted to North Carolina wines and the foods that complement them.

0:00 / 2:42
Instaread

MILL SPRING—Long before the Tryon Foothills appeared on a wine label, Tryon grapes had already made a name for themselves. 

In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, growers packed their fruit for markets far beyond Polk County, while vendors sold baskets to travelers passing through the Tryon railroad depot. The grape trade helped put this little corner of North Carolina on the map. 

On Friday, November 6, that history found a modern expression at Tryon International, where more than 200 guests attended Taste of NC, an evening devoted to North Carolina wines and the foods that complement them. 

Presented by the North Carolina Winegrowers Association, the event brought together 17 wine and beverage producers and 16 culinary partners. Guests moved among tasting stations, meeting the people behind the wines and sampling dishes created to bring out their character. 

Valerie Strotmeyer, visiting from Raleigh, came away impressed. 

“The wines are surprisingly good,” she said. “The foods were very complementary to let the wine really show off.”

Among the local culinary participants was Tryon’s own Huckleberry’s, where Michaila Lawter prepared apple butter and bourbon meatballs. The dish offered a seasonal nod to the state’s prolific apple-growing traditions, combining the fruit’s sweetness with the warmth of bourbon in a celebration of autumn flavors. 

Just over a year ago, the Tryon Foothills became a federally recognized American Viticultural Area, or AVA, encompassing approximately 176 square miles of Polk County. The designation recognizes the region’s distinctive grape-growing conditions and gives qualifying wines their own geographical identity. 

Presented by the North Carolina Winegrowers Association, the event brought together 17 wine and beverage producers and 16 culinary partners.

For Sofia Lilly, winemaker at Overmountain Vineyards, the gathering represented something considerably larger than another wine tasting. 

“I feel like we are on the cusp of redefining the reasons that people will want to travel to the area,” Lilly said. 

She also drew a connection between today’s winemakers and the growers who first established Tryon’s national reputation.

“One hundred years ago it was the railroad that took the name of Tryon grapes to the rest of America,” she said. “Now the Tryon Foothills AVA can show the nation that this is where great wines are being crafted with care and skill.” 

Organizers reported attendance exceeding 200 and expressed enthusiasm for Tryon International as a host venue. Having previously staged Taste of NC events in Raleigh and Wilmington, they indicated an interest in returning to Mill Spring next year. 

The gathering reminded everyone that its agricultural heritage remains a living tradition, cultivated by a new generation of growers, winemakers and chefs. 

A century ago, travelers carried Tryon grapes away by train. Today, visitors are coming to discover what those same foothills can offer by the glass.
